pairs.source_text: Omnis Caesareo cedit labor Amphitheatro, unum pro cunctis fama loquetur opus.
pairs.question: Cui operi omnia mundi miracula, pyramides et Babylona et Mausolea, cedere Martialis canit?
pairs.question_en: To what work does Martial sing that all the wonders of the world - the pyramids, Babylon, the Mausoleum - yield?
pairs.derivation: The opening claim of the book: the Flavian Amphitheatre surpasses the Seven Wonders. Anchored to the named Amphitheatrum Caesareum against named wonders; single short answer supported verbatim by 'Omnis Caesareo cedit labor Amphitheatro'. A celebrated, closed-book fact of Roman culture.

pairs.source_text: Barbara pyramidum sileat miracula Memphis, Assyrius iactet nec Babylona labor;
pairs.question: Cuius urbis Aegyptiae miracula sunt pyramides apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: To which Egyptian city do the marvels of the pyramids belong, according to Martial?
pairs.derivation: Martial assigns the pyramids to Memphis, the standard Roman association of the pyramids with that city. Entity-anchored (pyramids, Egypt, Martial); one-word verifiable answer; shared geographic knowledge of the ancient wonder list.

pairs.source_text: Hic ubi sidereus propius uidet astra colossus et crescunt media pegmata celsa uia, inuidiosa feri radiabant atria regis unaque iam tota stabat in urbe domus;
pairs.question: Quod simulacrum ingens iuxta Amphitheatrum Caesareum astra propius videre dicit Martialis?
pairs.question_en: What huge statue next to the Caesarean Amphitheatre does Martial say sees the stars more closely?
pairs.answer_en: The starry colossus (the Colossus of Nero).
pairs.derivation: The colossus standing beside the new amphitheatre - the famous Colossus that later gave the building its name. Anchored to the Amphitheatre and Martial; short named answer supported verbatim by 'sidereus propius uidet astra colossus'.

pairs.source_text: inuidiosa feri radiabant atria regis unaque iam tota stabat in urbe domus; hic ubi conspicui uenerabilis Amphitheatri erigitur moles, stagna Neronis erant;
pairs.question: Cuius principis domus una tota in urbe Roma stare dicebatur, priusquam Amphitheatrum Flavium erigeretur?
pairs.question_en: Which emperor's single house was said to stand in the whole city of Rome before the Flavian Amphitheatre was built?
pairs.derivation: Nero's Golden House filled the whole city ('una tota stabat in urbe domus'), the 'fierce king' being identified by 'stagna Neronis' in the next couplet. Anchored to Rome and Nero; famous closed-book fact about the site of the Colosseum.

pairs.source_text: hic ubi conspicui uenerabilis Amphitheatri erigitur moles, stagna Neronis erant;
pairs.question: Quo loco moles Amphitheatri Caesarei erecta est, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: On what spot was the mass of the Caesarean Amphitheatre raised, according to Martial?
pairs.answer_en: Where Nero's lake (the ponds of the Golden House) had been.
pairs.derivation: The Colosseum was built on the drained lake of Nero's domus Aurea - the most famous fact about its site, stated verbatim ('stagna Neronis erant'). Anchored to the Amphitheatre and Nero; short verifiable answer.

pairs.source_text: Vox diuersa sonat populorum, tum tamen una est, cum uerus patriae diceris esse pater.
pairs.question: Quo nomine populi omnium gentium una voce Caesarem in spectaculis appellant, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: By what name do the peoples of all nations with one voice address Caesar at the spectacles, according to Martial?
pairs.answer_en: True father of the fatherland (pater patriae).
pairs.derivation: The assembled nations, speaking different tongues, unite in acclaiming the emperor as pater patriae - the imperial title. Anchored to Caesar and the amphitheatre crowds; short titular answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Crinibus in nodum tortis uenere Sygambri, atque aliter tortis crinibus Aethiopes.
pairs.question: Quomodo Sygambri crines gestare dicuntur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: How are the Sygambri said to wear their hair, according to Martial?
pairs.derivation: The Germanic hair-knot (cf. the Suebian knot in Tacitus) attributed to the Sygambri among the spectators streaming to Rome. Ethnographic custom anchored to a named people; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Exulat Ausonia profugus delator ab urbe: haec licet inpensis principis adnumeres.
pairs.question: Quod hominum genus inter spectacula Amphitheatri Caesar ab urbe Roma in exilium egit, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: Which class of men did Caesar drive from the city of Rome into exile during the spectacles of the Amphitheatre, according to Martial?
pairs.derivation: At the opening games the informers were paraded in the arena and banished - a recorded act of Titus, counted by Martial among the emperor's gifts. Anchored to Caesar, Rome, the games; single-word answer supported verbatim by 'Exulat... delator ab urbe'.

pairs.source_text: Iunctam Pasiphaen Dictaeo credite tauro: uidimus, accepit fabula prisca fidem.
pairs.question: Quam feminam Dictaeo tauro iunctam in harena Caesaris visam esse Martialis testatur?
pairs.question_en: Which woman does Martial attest was seen joined to the Dictaean bull in Caesar's arena?
pairs.derivation: The arena staged the Pasiphae myth as a real show - 'credite: uidimus'. Anchored to the Dictaean bull, Caesar's arena, and Martial as witness; one-name answer supported verbatim. A famous instance of myth enacted as spectacle.

pairs.source_text: Prostratum uasta Nemees in ualle leonem nobile et Herculeum fama canebat opus. Prisca fides taceat: nam post tua munera, Caesar, hoc iam femineo Marte fatemur agi.
pairs.question: Quo Marte leo, quod olim Herculeum opus erat, in muneribus Caesaris prostratus est, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: By what kind of combat was a lion laid low at Caesar's games - the deed that was once the work of Hercules - according to Martial?
pairs.answer_en: By a woman's fighting - a woman did it.
pairs.derivation: A woman killed a lion in the arena, outdoing Hercules' Nemean feat ('femineo Marte'). Anchored to Caesar's munera and the Herculean comparison; short answer supported verbatim. Evidence for women fighting at the opening games.

pairs.source_text: Prostratum uasta Nemees in ualle leonem nobile et Herculeum fama canebat opus.
pairs.question: Quis heros leonem in valle Nemees prostravisse fama canebatur?
pairs.question_en: Which hero was famed in story to have laid low the lion in the valley of Nemea?
pairs.derivation: The Nemean lion as Hercules' celebrated labor - canonical shared myth, evidenced verbatim ('Herculeum... opus'). Anchored to Nemea; one-name answer.

pairs.source_text: nuda Caledonia sic uiscera praebuit urso non falsa pendens in cruce Laureolus.
pairs.question: Cui ferae Laureolus, in cruce non falsa pendens, nuda viscera in harena praebuit?
pairs.question_en: To what beast did Laureolus, hanging on a cross that was not fake, offer his bare flesh in the arena?
pairs.derivation: The Laureolus mime staged as a real execution: a condemned man on a real cross exposed to a Caledonian bear. Anchored to the named Laureolus; short answer supported verbatim. Famous instance of fatal charades at the opening games.

pairs.source_text: Qualiter in Scythica religatus rupe Prometheus adsiduam nimio pectore pauit auem,
pairs.question: In qua rupe religatus Prometheus avem adsiduam pectore suo pavit?
pairs.question_en: On what rock was Prometheus bound as he fed the unrelenting bird with his breast?
pairs.derivation: The canonical Prometheus myth - bound on a Scythian crag, feeding the bird - cited by Martial as the pattern for the Laureolus punishment. Anchored to Prometheus; short place answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Daedale, Lucano cum sic lacereris ab urso, quam cuperes pinnas nunc habuisse tuas!
pairs.question: A qua fera Daedalus in spectaculis Caesaris laceratus est, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: By what beast was Daedalus torn apart at Caesar's spectacles, according to Martial?
pairs.derivation: Another mythological charade made real: a 'Daedalus' mangled by a Lucanian bear, Martial joking that he must wish he had his wings. Anchored to Daedalus; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Praestitit exhibitus tota tibi, Caesar, harena quae non promisit proelia rhinoceros. O quam terribilis exarsit pronus in iras! Quantus erat taurus, cui pila taurus erat!
pairs.question: Cui ferae taurus in harena Caesaris quasi pila fuit, ut canit Martialis?
pairs.question_en: To what beast was a bull like a mere training-dummy in Caesar's arena, as Martial sings?
pairs.derivation: The rhinoceros exhibited at the games tossed a bull as if it were a pila (straw dummy used to bait bulls). Anchored to Caesar's arena and the named beast; one-word answer supported verbatim by 'cui pila taurus erat'.

pairs.source_text: Laeserat ingrato leo perfidus ore magistrum, ausus tam notas contemerare manus, sed dignas tanto persoluit crimine poenas, et qui non tulerat uerbera, tela tulit.
pairs.question: Quam poenam leo, qui ore perfido magistrum suum in harena laeserat, persolvit?
pairs.question_en: What punishment did the lion pay that had wounded its own trainer with treacherous jaws in the arena?
pairs.answer_en: It suffered the weapons - it was killed with spears.
pairs.derivation: Arena discipline: a lion that mauled its magister was executed with weapons ('qui non tulerat uerbera, tela tulit'). Anchored to the lion-and-trainer episode at Caesar's games; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Praeceps sanguinea dum se rotat ursus harena, inplicitam uisco perdidit ille fugam.
pairs.question: Qua re ursus in harena Caesaris captus fugam perdidit, ut narrat Martialis?
pairs.question_en: By what means did a bear in Caesar's arena lose its escape, as Martial tells?
pairs.derivation: A bear was taken in the arena with birdlime, hunted like a bird ('aucupis arte' in the following lines). Anchored to the bear at the games; short answer supported verbatim by 'inplicitam uisco perdidit... fugam'.

pairs.source_text: Inter Caesareae discrimina saeua Dianae fixisset grauidam cum leuis hasta suem, exiluit partus miserae de uulnere matris.
pairs.question: Unde partus suis gravidae, hasta in harena transfixae, exiluit apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: From where did the offspring of a pregnant sow, pierced by a spear in the arena, leap out, according to Martial?
pairs.derivation: The famous marvel of the venatio: a piglet born through the death-wound of its speared mother. Anchored to the Caesarean hunt (Caesareae Dianae) and the sow; short answer supported verbatim by 'exiluit partus... de uulnere matris'.

pairs.source_text: Quis negat esse satum materno funere Bacchum? sic genitum numen credite: nata fera est.
pairs.question: Quis deus materno funere satus esse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Which god is said in tradition to have been born at his mother's death?
pairs.derivation: Bacchus born at the death of his mother Semele - canonical shared myth, cited by Martial as parallel to the sow's piglet. Anchored to the named god; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Summa tuae, Meleagre, fuit quae gloria famae, quantast Carpophori portio, fusus aper! Ille et praecipiti uenabula condidit urso, primus in Arctoi qui fuit arce poli, strauit et ignota spectandum mole leonem, herculeas potuit qui decuisse manus, et uolucrem longo porrexit uulnere pardum.
pairs.question: Cuius venatoris in harena Caesaris parva tantum portio fuit aper fusus, quae summa Meleagri gloria fuerat?
pairs.question_en: For which beast-hunter in Caesar's arena was a slain boar - once the whole glory of Meleager - only a small part of his record?
pairs.derivation: Carpophorus, the star bestiarius of the opening games, killed boar, bear, lion and pard, dwarfing Meleager's fame. Anchored to the named hunter and Meleager; one-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Vexerat Europen fraterna per aequora taurus: at nunc Alciden taurus in astra tulit.
pairs.question: Quam virginem taurus per aequora vexisse fama canitur?
pairs.question_en: Which maiden is a bull famed to have carried across the seas?
pairs.derivation: Jupiter as bull carrying Europa over the sea ('fraterna aequora' - his brother Neptune's realm) - canonical shared myth, quoted as foil for the arena bull. Anchored to Europa and the bull; one-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: at nunc Alciden taurus in astra tulit. Caesaris atque Iouis confer nunc, fama, iuuencos: par onus ut tulerint, altius iste tulit.
pairs.question: Quem heroa taurus in harena Caesaris in astra sustulit, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: Which hero did a bull lift to the stars in Caesar's arena, according to Martial?
pairs.derivation: An arena stunt: a bull hoisted a performer playing Hercules (Alcides) skyward, outdoing Jove's bull that carried Europa. Anchored to Caesar's arena and the named hero; short answer supported verbatim by 'Alciden taurus in astra tulit'.

pairs.source_text: Quod pius et supplex elephas te, Caesar, adorat hic modo qui tauro tam metuendus erat, non facit hoc iussus, nulloque docente magistro, crede mihi, nostrum sentit et ille deum.
pairs.question: Quae belua in harena Caesarem supplex adoravit, non iussa nulloque docente magistro?
pairs.question_en: Which beast knelt in supplication before Caesar in the arena, unbidden and with no trainer teaching it?
pairs.derivation: The famous kneeling elephant of the opening games, which Martial insists acted of its own accord. Anchored to Caesar and the arena; one-word answer supported verbatim by 'non facit hoc iussus, nulloque docente magistro'.

pairs.source_text: Lambere securi dextram consueta magistri tigris, ab Hyrcano gloria rara iugo, saeua ferum rabido lacerauit dente leonem: res noua, non ullis cognita temporibus.
pairs.question: Quae fera, ab Hyrcano iugo adducta, leonem in harena rabido dente laceravit, quod nullis ante temporibus cognitum erat?
pairs.question_en: Which beast, brought from the Hyrcanian ridge, mangled a lion in the arena with raging teeth - a thing never known in any age before?
pairs.derivation: The tame Hyrcanian tigress that savaged a lion, billed by Martial as unprecedented ('res noua'). Anchored to Hyrcania, the lion, and the arena; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ausa est tale nihil, siluis dum uixit in altis: postquam inter nos est, plus feritatis habet.
pairs.question: Ubi tigris Hyrcana plus feritatis habere dicitur apud Martialem, in silvis altis an inter homines?
pairs.question_en: Where does Martial say the Hyrcanian tigress has more ferocity - in the deep forests or among men?
pairs.derivation: Martial's pointed claim about the lion-mauling tigress: it dared nothing like this in the wild and grew fiercer among men. Anchored to the Hyrcanian tigress episode; short two-way verifiable answer supported verbatim by 'postquam inter nos est, plus feritatis habet'.

pairs.source_text: Qui modo per totam flammis stimulatus harenam sustulerat raptas taurus in astra pilas. Occubuit tandem cornuto adore petitus, dum facilem tolli sic elephanta putat.
pairs.question: Quam beluam taurus, qui pilas in astra iactaverat, aeque facilem tolli frustra putavit atque occubuit?
pairs.question_en: What beast did the bull that had tossed straw dummies to the stars vainly think just as easy to toss - and so fell?
pairs.derivation: The bull that hurled the pilae skyward died when it attacked an elephant, thinking it could toss it too. Anchored to the bull-and-elephant bout at the games; one-word answer supported verbatim by 'facilem tolli sic elephanta putat'.

pairs.source_text: Cum peteret pars haec Myrinum, pars illa Triumphum, promisit pariter Caesar utraque manu.
pairs.question: Quos duos harenae artifices, cum populus partibus diversis posceret, Caesar utraque manu pariter promisit?
pairs.question_en: Which two arena performers, demanded by rival sections of the crowd, did Caesar promise together with both hands?
pairs.derivation: The crowd split between two named favorites; Caesar granted both, one with each hand. Anchored to the two named performers and Caesar; two-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quidquid in Orpheo Rhodope spectasse theatro dicitur, exhibuit, Caesar, harena tibi. Repserunt scopuli mirandaque silua cucurrit, quale fuisse nemus creditur Hesperidum. Adfuit inmixtum pecori genus omne ferarum et supra uatem multa pependit auis, ipse sed ingrato iacuit laceratus ab urso.
pairs.question: A qua fera Orpheus, fabulam suam in harena Caesaris agens, contra fabulam laceratus iacuit?
pairs.question_en: By what beast did Orpheus, playing out his own story in Caesar's arena, lie mangled - contrary to the story?
pairs.derivation: The Orpheus pageant - creeping rocks, running woods, beasts and birds charmed - ended with the condemned 'Orpheus' torn by a bear, which Martial notes was contrary to the myth. Anchored to Orpheus and Caesar's arena; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Orphea quod subito tellus emisit hiatu ursam elisuram, uenit ab Eurydice.
pairs.question: Quo modo ursa, quae Orphea in harena Caesaris elisura erat, emissa est?
pairs.question_en: How was the she-bear sent forth that was to crush Orpheus in Caesar's arena?
pairs.answer_en: Through a sudden chasm in the earth.
pairs.derivation: Stage machinery of the fatal Orpheus show: the bear rose through a trap - a sudden opening of the ground - which Martial jokes came 'from Eurydice' below. Anchored to Orpheus and the arena; short answer supported verbatim by 'subito tellus emisit hiatu'.

pairs.source_text: Namque grauem cornu gemino sic extulit ursum, iactat ut inpositas taurus in astra pilas:
pairs.question: Quam feram rhinoceros in harena Caesaris cornu gemino ita extulit ut taurus pilas iactat?
pairs.question_en: What beast did the rhinoceros in Caesar's arena lift with its double horn just as a bull tosses straw dummies?
pairs.derivation: The rhinoceros (named at the epigram's start, 'rhinocerota') hoisted a heavy bear on its twin horn like a bull tossing pilae - also evidence that Martial's beast was the two-horned rhinoceros. Anchored to the rhinoceros at Caesar's games; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Norica tam certo uenabula dirigit ictu fortis adhuc teneri dextera Carpophori.
pairs.question: Cuiatia venabula Carpophorus venator certo ictu direxisse dicitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: Hunting-spears of what origin is the hunter Carpophorus said in Martial to have aimed with unerring stroke?
pairs.derivation: Carpophorus wields Norican venabula - Noricum's iron and steel being proverbially the best. Anchored to the named hunter; one-word answer supported verbatim. Also attests that Carpophorus was still young ('adhuc teneri').

pairs.source_text: ne te decipiat ratibus naualis Enyo et par unda fretis, hic modo terra fuit. Non credis? specta, dum lassant aequora Martem: parua mora est, dices 'Hic modo pontus erat.'
pairs.question: Quale spectaculum Caesar in Amphitheatro eo loco edidit ubi modo terra fuerat, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: What kind of spectacle did Caesar stage in the Amphitheatre on the very spot where just now there had been dry land, according to Martial?
pairs.answer_en: A naval battle, with water let in.
pairs.derivation: The flooded arena: sea-fights ('naualis Enyo') with real ships where there had just been land, then land again ('Hic modo pontus erat'). Anchored to Caesar's Amphitheatre; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quod nocturna tibi, Leandre, pepercerit unda desine mirari: Caesaris unda fuit.
pairs.question: Cuius unda fuisse dicitur quae Leandro natanti in spectaculis pepercit, ut iocatur Martialis?
pairs.question_en: Whose water is it said to have been that spared the swimming Leander at the spectacles, as Martial jokes?
pairs.derivation: A performer swam the Leander role in the flooded arena and lived; Martial's point is that the wave spared him because it was Caesar's water. Anchored to Leander and Caesar; one-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Cum peteret dulces audax Leandros amores et fessus tumidis iam premeretur aquis, sic miser instantes adfatus dicitur undas: 'Parcite dum propero, mergite cum redeo.'
pairs.question: Quo tempore Leander undas se mergere passurum dixisse fertur - dum ad amores properaret, an cum rediret?
pairs.question_en: At what moment did Leander reportedly tell the waves they might drown him - while hurrying to his love, or on his way back?
pairs.derivation: The famous Leander mot: spare me as I hasten there, drown me when I return. Anchored to the named Leander; short two-way verifiable answer supported verbatim by 'Parcite dum propero, mergite cum redeo'.

pairs.source_text: Lusit Nereidum docilis chorus aequore toto et uario faciles ordine pinxit aquas. Fuscina dente minax recto fuit, ancora curuo: credidimus remum credidimusque ratem,
pairs.question: Quis chorus in aquis spectaculorum Caesaris lusit et figuras - fuscinam, ancoram, remum, ratem - in aequore pinxit?
pairs.question_en: What chorus performed in the waters of Caesar's spectacles and traced figures - a trident, an anchor, an oar, a ship - on the surface?
pairs.answer_en: A trained chorus of Nereids (synchronized swimmers).
pairs.derivation: The aquatic ballet of the flooded arena: swimmers as Nereids forming pictures on the water. Anchored to Caesar's water shows and the named figures; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: et gratum nautis sidus fulgere Laconum lataque perspicuo uela tumere sinu.
pairs.question: Quorum sidus nautis gratum esse Martialis dicit?
pairs.question_en: Whose constellation does Martial call welcome to sailors?
pairs.answer_en: That of the Laconians (the Spartan twins Castor and Pollux).
pairs.derivation: The 'star of the Laconians' - the Dioscuri, patrons of sailors - among the shapes the Nereids traced. The twins' star as the sailors' friend is ambient Roman religious-mythological knowledge; anchored by 'sidus Laconum', short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Herculeae laudis numeretur gloria: plus est bis denas pariter perdomuisse feras.
pairs.question: Quot feras Carpophorus in harena Caesaris pariter perdomuisse dicitur apud Martialem?
pairs.question_en: How many beasts is Carpophorus said in Martial to have subdued at once in Caesar's arena?
pairs.derivation: The count that caps the Carpophorus panegyric (the epigram opens 'Saecula Carpophorum, Caesar, si prisca tulissent'): twenty beasts mastered together, more than Hercules' glory. Anchored to Carpophorus; number answer supported verbatim by 'bis denas pariter perdomuisse feras'.

pairs.source_text: Saecula Carpophorum, Caesar, si prisca tulissent, non Porthaoniam barbara terra feram, non Marathon taurum, Nemee frondosa leonem, Arcas Maenalium non timuisset aprum.
pairs.question: Quae terra taurum fabulosum timuisse dicitur apud Martialem, sicut Nemee frondosa leonem?
pairs.question_en: What land is said in Martial to have feared a fabled bull, just as leafy Nemea feared the lion?
pairs.derivation: The canonical myth-place pairing of the bull of Marathon, listed beside Nemea's lion and Arcadia's Maenalian boar as terrors Carpophorus would have spared the old world. Anchored to Marathon and Nemea; one-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Si uetus aequorei reuocetur fabula monstri, Hesionen soluet solus et Andromedan.
pairs.question: Quae duae virgines in fabulis monstris aequoreis expositae erant, quas solus Carpophorus solvere posset, ut ait Martialis?
pairs.question_en: Which two maidens were in the myths exposed to sea monsters, whom Carpophorus alone could set free, as Martial says?
pairs.derivation: The two canonical maidens of the sea-monster myths (freed by Hercules and Perseus respectively), invoked as the measure of Carpophorus. Anchored to both named heroines; two-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Igniferos possit sine Colchide iungere tauros, possit utramque feram uincere Pasiphaes.
pairs.question: Sine cuius feminae auxilio Carpophorus igniferos tauros iungere posset, ut canit Martialis?
pairs.question_en: Without which woman's help could Carpophorus have yoked the fire-breathing bulls, as Martial sings?
pairs.answer_en: Without the Colchian - that is, Medea.
pairs.derivation: In the shared myth the fire-breathing bulls were yoked only with the Colchian Medea's help; Martial says Carpophorus would not have needed her. Anchored to the fiery bulls and 'Colchis'; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Augusti labor hic fuerat committere classes et freta nauali sollicitare tuba. Caesaris haec nostri pars est quota?
pairs.question: Cuius principis labor antea fuerat classes committere et freta navali tuba sollicitare, ut Martialis memorat?
pairs.question_en: Which emperor's achievement had it previously been to set fleets in battle and rouse the waters with the naval trumpet, as Martial recalls?
pairs.derivation: Augustus' famous naumachia, named as the older benchmark that Caesar's water spectacle dwarfs. Anchored to Augustus and the naumachia; one-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Fucinus et diri taceantur stagna Neronis: hanc norint unam saecula naumachiam.
pairs.question: Quae duo priorum principum naumachiarum loca taceri iubet Martialis prae naumachia Caesaris?
pairs.question_en: Which two sites of earlier emperors' naval shows does Martial bid be silent before Caesar's naumachia?
pairs.answer_en: The Fucine lake and Nero's pools.
pairs.derivation: The two named predecessors - the Fucinus (Claudius' lake naumachia) and the pools of 'dread Nero' - dismissed so that the ages may know this one naumachia. Anchored to both named sites; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quidquid et in Circo spectatur et Amphitheatro, id diues, Caesar, praestitit unda tibi.
pairs.question: Quorum duorum locorum spectacula unda naumachiae Caesaris pariter praestitit, teste Martiale?
pairs.question_en: The spectacles of which two venues did the water of Caesar's naumachia alike supply, according to Martial?
pairs.answer_en: Of the Circus and the Amphitheatre.
pairs.derivation: The water show reproduced everything seen in the Circus (even chariots on the waves, per the preceding lines) and in the Amphitheatre. Anchored to the two named venues and Caesar; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Cum traheret Priscus, traheret certamina Verus, esset et aequalis Mars utriusque diu, missio saepe uiris magno clamore petita est; sed Caesar legi paruit ipse suae; - lex erat, ad digitum posita concurrere parma: - quod licuit, lances donaque saepe dedit. Inuentus tamen est finis discriminis aequi: pugnauere pares, subcubuere pares. Misit utrique rudes et palmas Caesar utrique: hoc pretium uirtus ingeniosa tulit. Contigit hoc nullo nisi te sub principe, Caesar: cum duo pugnarent, uictor uterque fuit.
pairs.question: Qui duo gladiatores in muneribus Caesaris tam diu pari Marte pugnaverunt ut uterque victor discederet?
pairs.question_en: Which two gladiators fought so long on equal terms at Caesar's games that both walked away victors?
pairs.derivation: The most famous fact of the book: the drawn duel of Priscus and Verus, ended by Caesar declaring both victorious - 'cum duo pugnarent, uictor uterque fuit'. Anchored to the two named gladiators and Caesar; two-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Misit utrique rudes et palmas Caesar utrique: hoc pretium uirtus ingeniosa tulit.
pairs.question: Quae praemia Caesar et Prisco et Vero, pari Marte pugnantibus, utrique misit?
pairs.question_en: What prizes did Caesar send to both Priscus and Verus, who had fought on equal terms?
pairs.answer_en: The wooden swords of discharge (rudes) and the palms of victory.
pairs.derivation: Both gladiators received the rudis - the wooden sword marking discharge from the arena - and the victor's palm. Anchored to Priscus, Verus, and Caesar; brief noun-phrase answer supported verbatim. Core gladiatorial custom (rudis = discharge, palma = victory).

pairs.source_text: sed Caesar legi paruit ipse suae; - lex erat, ad digitum posita concurrere parma: - quod licuit, lances donaque saepe dedit.
pairs.question: Quae lex pugnae in munere Caesaris posita erat, cui Caesar ipse paruit, ut refert Martialis?
pairs.question_en: What rule of combat was laid down at Caesar's games, which Caesar himself obeyed, as Martial reports?
pairs.answer_en: To fight on, the shield set aside, until a finger was raised (the signal of surrender).
pairs.derivation: The stated lex of the Priscus-Verus bout: the fight ran 'ad digitum' - until the raised finger of submission - and even the emperor bound himself to his own rule. Gladiatorial convention, culturally salient; anchored to Caesar's munus; brief answer quoted from the source.

pairs.source_text: Concita ueloces fugeret cum damma Molossos et uaria lentas necteret arte moras, Caesaris ante pedes supplex similisque roganti constitit, et praedam non tetigere canes.
pairs.question: Ante cuius pedes damma, veloces Molossos fugiens, supplex constitit, ita ut canes praedam non tangerent?
pairs.question_en: Before whose feet did the hind, fleeing the swift Molossian hounds, halt as a suppliant, so that the dogs did not touch their prey?
pairs.derivation: The suppliant hind of the venatio: chased by Molossian hounds, it stopped as if begging before the emperor, and the dogs spared it - Martial's proof of Caesar's numen. Anchored to Caesar and the named Molossian breed; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Flauia gens, quantum tibi tertius abstulit heres! paene fuit tanti, non habuisse duos.
pairs.question: Quotus heres genti Flaviae tantum abstulisse dicitur ut paene tanti fuerit duos priores non habuisse?
pairs.question_en: Which heir in order is said to have taken so much from the Flavian house that it would almost have been worth not having the former two?
pairs.derivation: The bitter closing couplet on the gens Flavia: its third heir (Domitian, after Vespasian and Titus) disgraced it. Anchored to the named Flavian house; ordinal answer supported verbatim by 'tertius abstulit heres'.
